extracted.intended_audience: educated English reading public (readers of The Spectator, early 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A periodical-essay set of prescriptive comments and letters offering standards for clear English usage, honest narration, moral responsibility in authorship, pedagogy, and public behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid foreign phrases; preserve English idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain Men might be set apart as Superintendants of our Language, to hinder any Words of a Foreign Coin from passing among us; and in particular to prohibit any French Phrases from becoming Current in this Kingdom, when those of our own Stamp are altogether as valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use native English expressions instead of imported French phrases; be vigilant against war- or fashion-driven adoptions that adulterate the tongue. Example/anecdote: the present War has so Adulterated our Tongue with strange Words that it would be impossible for one of our Great Grandfathers to know what his Posterity have been doing, were he to read their Exploits in a Modern News Paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report military and public news in plain English
rubrics_metrics.description: The English cannot be too clear in their Narrative of those Actions... When we have won Battles which may be described in our own Language, why are our Papers filled with so many unintelligible Exploits?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid technical or foreign jargon in newspaper accounts when plain English will do; provide translations or secretaries for soldiers so the public can understand campaigns. Example: soldiers' letters full of jargon (drum, trumpet, Charte Blanche) left civilians puzzled until prints repeated the terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit foreign technical terms only when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: I do make some Allowances for this Part of the War, Fortifications having been foreign Inventions, and upon that Account abounding in foreign Terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept foreign words where the concept is newly introduced or technical and lacks an established English equivalent; otherwise prefer English words to preserve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and intelligibility as a duty of writers/journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Commanders lose half their Praise, and our People half their Joy, by means of those hard Words and dark Expressions in which our News Papers do so much abound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write so readers can grasp events and praise; avoid 'hard Words and dark Expressions' that obscure meaning. The anecdote of the father and the curate demonstrates the social cost of unintelligible prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility of the author; avoid corrupting posterity
rubrics_metrics.description: How careful should an Author be of committing any thing to Print that may corrupt Posterity, and poison the Minds of Men with Vice and Error? Writers of great Talents, who employ their Parts in propagating Immorality ... are to be looked upon as the Pests of Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before publishing, consider whether the work promotes vice or error; avoid seasoning vicious sentiments with wit. The piece frames immoral writers as positively harmful across generations and uses the notion (satirical) of prolonged punishment to emphasize the duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the longevity and lasting influence of books
rubrics_metrics.description: Books are the Legacies that a great Genius leaves to Mankind... they may last as long as the Sun and Moon... How careful should an Author be of committing any thing to Print that may corrupt Posterity?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should weigh the long-term effects of their printed words because books endure far longer than other arts; this is both a warning and a call for prudence in subject and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in narrative; avoid inventing or embellishing facts
rubrics_metrics.description: He was unable to contain himself... from adding a few Circumstances to enliven plain Narrative. ... forms Incidents which should have happened to have pleased him in the Story. One is a Prating, the other a Silent Liar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not invent incidents to enliven or embellish ordinary matters, especially in accounts purporting to be true; distinguish harmless fancy from deliberate falsehood. Negative examples: correspondents who invent public and notorious falsehoods are censured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schoolmasters' conduct: politeness, method, and avoidance of cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: We might then possibly see Learning become a Pleasure, and Children delighting themselves in that which now they abhor... 'Tis pity but we had a Set of Men, polite in their Behaviour and Method of Teaching, who should be put into a Condition of being above flattering or fearing the Parents of those they instruct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should be courteous and skilled in pedagogy, avoid excessive corporal punishment, and be insulated from parental influence that encourages harsh methods; the aim is to make learning pleasurable and to prevent broken spirits and lost potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote genuine learning over pedantry and rote
rubrics_metrics.description: We might then possibly see Learning become a Pleasure ... we should have no more Pedants, nor any bred to Learning who had not Genius for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate teaching practices that encourage understanding and taste rather than mechanical pedantry; avoid producing scholars who merely mimic learning without talent or judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve decency in public assemblies; penalize disruptive behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: For preserving therefore the Decency of publick Assemblies, methinks it would be but reasonable that those who Disturb others should pay at least a double Price for their Places; or rather Women of Birth and Distinction should be informed that a Levity of Behaviour ... degrades them below their meanest Attendants; and Gentlemen should know that a fine Coat is a Livery, when the Person who wears it discovers no higher Sense than that of a Footman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage sets of whisperers, laughers, and otherwise impertinent groups in public entertainments by social sanctions or pricing; urge the well-born to behave with decorum so assemblies are not distracted by trivial or coarse behaviour.
